quote: all of whom insist that if their metaethic is untrue, then morality falls apart
content: The imagined panel is a caricature. Most professional metaethicists don't hold that morality collapses if their theory is false. Quasi-realists such as Blackburn and Gibbard built whole research programs on showing that ordinary moral practice survives without robust realism, and realists typically say the same about their rivals. Moral realism was the majority view in the 2020 PhilPapers survey (Bourget & Chalmers 2023), and its holders mostly wouldn't describe their theory as the only thing keeping them from killing. The essay's audience of anxious metaethicists comes from blog comments, not from the field.

quote: Otherwise you would be committing what is known (appropriately) as The Genetic Fallacy: causation is not the same concept as justification.
content: Evolutionary debunking arguments are not genetic fallacies, and the most influential one explains why. Street (2006) argues that selection shaped our evaluative dispositions for fitness, not for tracking independent moral truth. Unless realists can explain why tracking fitness and tracking truth coincide, that causal story undermines the justification, as it would for any belief produced by a process insensitive to its truth. The book is also inconsistent here. "Where Recursive Justification Hits Bottom" uses the causal story of evolution to vindicate induction, and this essay forbids anyone to use the same kind of story to impugn morality.

quote: Maybe that which you would do even if there were no morality, is your morality.
content: This contradicts the book's own metaethics two essays later. "Morality as Fixed Computation" insists that "right" is not "What will I decide to do?" That question belongs to the Type 2 calculator, whose output is correct just because it is its output. Defining morality as whatever you would do anyway is exactly the Type 2 calculator. The line of retreat offered here is the position the sequence later calls a world-destroying design error.

quote: There’s a difference between a calculator that calculates “What is 2 + 3?” and one that outputs “What do I output when someone presses ‘2,’ ‘+,’ and ‘3’?”
content: The calculator analogy presupposes what the view denies. A calculator computing "2 + 3" answers a question whose answer is fixed independently of any calculator, which is why it can be wrong. On the book's metaethics there is no such independent fact; the "question" is defined by what is implemented in human brains. That makes the moral calculator more like one asking "what would calculators of my make output under idealization," which is a question about calculators, and the reassurance that morality is "not about your thoughts" evaporates. The Moral Twin Earth literature presses this objection against analytic descriptivism (Horgan & Timmons 1992).
